summary: Parallel NFS lets clients access file data directly on storage devices, bypassing the NFSv4 server. The block storage specification is RFC 5663, and this RFC addresses how the disks used with it are protected.

plainLanguage.summary: When many people use shared storage directly, they can hurt each other's data. This adds safety measures.

questions: how are pnfs block disks protected
what is pnfs block disk protection
what is the pnfs block gpt guid
why do pnfs clients need to identify disks at boot
subtitle: A partition-table label that lets a computer recognise shared pNFS block disks at boot, before it can ask the server.

tldr.problem: A client operating system normally scans and activates block devices before its NFS client starts, so it could modify a pNFS block device (for example by mounting or initializing a local filesystem) before it has contacted the server.
tldr.mechanism: Each block device dedicated to pNFS carries a GUID partition table (GPT), and the pNFS partitions are labelled with the GUID e5b72a69-23e5-4b4d-b176-16532674fc34, which any host can check without talking to the server.
tldr.outcome: An operating system that recognises the GUID can keep non-pNFS access away from these disks from the moment it boots. The RFC updates RFC 5663.

today: RFC 6688 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2012 that updates RFC 5663. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Parallel NFS (pNFS) extends NFSv4 so that clients can reach file data directly on storage devices and bypass the NFSv4 server. RFC 6688 updates RFC 5663, the pNFS block layout specification, with a way to identify block storage devices used by pNFS without communicating with the server.

The goal is to let clients control access to those block devices when the client first boots, instead of waiting until it can talk to the NFSv4 server.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers share one big storage room. This document gives each shared storage disk a label, so a computer can tell it is special as soon as it wakes up.

sections.title: pNFS Architecture and Terms
sections.content:
In a pNFS system, clients speak NFSv4.1 with pNFS to a MetaData Server (MDS). The MDS is the NFSv4 server that hands out pNFS layouts and handles file metadata such as names and attributes. Clients then use a storage protocol to reach the storage devices directly, while a control protocol links the MDS and the storage devices.

The RFC uses 'storage device' as a general term for a data server or storage server for any pNFS layout type.
sections.plainLanguage: A teacher (the metadata server) tells each student which shelf to use, and then the students go to the shelves themselves.

sections.title: The Boot-Time Window of Vulnerability
sections.content:
Under RFC 5663, a client can only identify pNFS block devices by contacting the MDS to get device signature information. The client cannot do this reliably alone, because the location and contents of a device signature are chosen by the MDS, not the client.

Typical operating system boot code scans and activates block devices (for example SCSI) before the NFS client starts. That leaves a window in which the OS may modify a pNFS block device without contacting the server, for example by trying to mount or initialize a local filesystem on it.

Storage area network (SAN) access controls such as LUN mapping or masking could close the window, but they are quasi-static: they are usually configured once and not changed after crashes and reboots. The RFC says they can be changed for unusual cases, such as fencing (removing access from) an uncooperative client, but should not be part of routine operations like a reboot. A different mechanism is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: When a computer wakes up, it likes to check every disk and start using it. Without a warning label it might scribble on a disk that belongs to the whole group.

sections.title: The GPT Partition Table Entry
sections.content:
The fix is an entry in the GUID partition table (GPT). Each block storage device dedicated to pNFS includes a GPT, and the pNFS block storage partitions are identified in it with the GUID e5b72a69-23e5-4b4d-b176-16532674fc34, which was generated for this purpose.

The RFC notes that GPT GUID usage is well understood and implemented, and that no central registration mechanism exists for GPT GUIDs, or GUIDs in general, by design (see RFC 4122). It also says many current operating system versions support the GPT.

The entry is meant for shared pNFS storage devices that pNFS clients and servers can reach and that other hosts or systems may be able to reach as well. It lets all of them avoid accessing the devices by means other than pNFS.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is a long, one-of-a-kind code written in the disk's table of contents. Any computer can read it right away and know the disk is for the group.

sections.title: What Servers, Clients and Other Hosts Should Do
sections.content:
Servers that support pNFS block layouts SHOULD use the GPT and this GUID for all pNFS block storage devices.

A pNFS client operating system that supports block layouts SHOULD recognize the GUID and SHOULD use its presence to prevent data access to pNFS block devices until a layout that includes the device is received from the MDS. This lets the OS block non-pNFS access immediately upon boot.

Hosts and systems that do not support pNFS block layouts can add a check for the GUID too. If pNFS block devices are presented to them by mistake, the check can prevent writes that could otherwise corrupt the stored pNFS data.
sections.plainLanguage: The group's teacher puts the sticker on every shared disk. Each computer promises not to touch a stickered disk until the teacher gives it permission.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The pNFS block layout security considerations in RFC 5663 apply to this document. The security considerations in RFC 4122 apply to the GUID specified here.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules that already applied to the shared storage room still apply, and so do the rules for the special code.
